description: We’re a team from North Carolina in the United States, and we really enjoy building things. Between us we have experience in programming, robotics, app development and working with data, and we’re really excited to use NASA data to work on a real problem this weekend.
summary:
We developed Plume, a web app that uses NASA FIRMS fire data from the MODIS and VIIRS satellite instruments to show how much fire any area has had, month by month, since 2000. You draw an area on a map, and Plume builds a burning calendar for it. The calendar marks the peak months and years and compares this month with every past year.

Plume directly addresses the challenge. MODIS, on NASA's Terra and Aqua satellites, has recorded fires since 2000, but those satellites are being retired. VIIRS, which replaces it, sees finer detail and counts about twice as much fire over the same ground. Joined end to end, the two records make California's fire activity look like it jumped two and a half times in 2012. In Argentina's Gran Chaco they show fire rising when it actually fell. Plume converts MODIS into VIIRS terms using the years when both watched the same fires. When Suomi NPP stopped sending data in November 2026, Plume continued the record with NOAA-20. Tested on years it never saw, its yearly totals were off by 6.6% on average in California.

This matters because responders need a long fire history they can trust to tell whether a season is normal.
details:
What does it do?

Plume answers a question fire managers ask every season: is this normal for here? You draw an area on the map (a box, a polygon or a circle) or type in coordinates, then pick a date range. Plume then shows:

  • a burning calendar with one square per month since November 2000, shaded by how much fire the satellites saw
  • the peak months and years, the months furthest from normal, and the trend per decade
  • this month so far, compared with the same days of that month in every past year
  • a short plain-language summary of those numbers
  • You can download the results as CSV files, from the individual fire detections to the full calendar with its uncertainty ranges.

How does it work?

A MODIS pixel is about 1 km across and a VIIRS pixel about 375 m, so VIIRS catches small fires that MODIS misses. Plume makes the two records comparable in four steps:

  1. Clean. Keep vegetation fires at each instrument's recommended confidence level and remove duplicate detections where satellite passes overlap. Drop the heat from gas flares, factories and volcanoes.
  2. Grid. Count fire cell-days, meaning how many 5 km grid squares had fire on each day. This removes most of the difference in pixel size.
  3. Convert. Learn how MODIS maps to VIIRS from 2012 to 2019, when Aqua's MODIS and Suomi NPP's VIIRS passed over at nearly the same time of day. Each region and month gets its own fit. Weak and intense fires are handled separately, because VIIRS adds far more detections around small fires.
  4. Fill the ends. Scale up the months before July 2002, when only Terra was flying. Use NOAA-20 to continue the record after Suomi NPP stopped sending data on 2 November 2026.

Every converted month comes with an uncertainty range.

Does it work?

We tested the conversion on data it had never seen:

  • Leaving out one year at a time, yearly totals were off by 6.6% on average in California and 3.6% in the Gran Chaco.
  • Training on half the grid squares and testing on the other half, the errors were 7.4% and 2.6%.
  • Continuing the record with NOAA-20, the errors were 2.3% and 2.8%.

The app also shows where the method falls short. From 2020, as the MODIS satellites drifted to earlier passes, our predictions ran 6.5% low in California.

The calendar also picks out real disasters. In our record, 2020 is California's busiest year, and that September had eight times the fire of a typical September.

What benefits does it have?

  • Fire managers can plan crews around the months that actually burn.
  • Responders can see early when a season is running far above normal.
  • Land managers can tell whether burning in their area is going up or down.
  • Scientists get a consistent series they can download and check.

What is the intended impact?

Without this correction, people who use fire history either drop the twelve years before VIIRS or read a jump in fire that never happened. In the Gran Chaco, the raw joined data says fire rose by half across 2012. Once corrected, it fell by about a quarter. As MODIS shuts down, Plume keeps 25 years of fire history usable for the people who plan around it.

How is it creative?

  • Fire cell-days is a unit we designed. It makes the two instruments comparable before any conversion.
  • Splitting fires by intensity lets the conversion follow each year's mix of small and large fires instead of applying one flat ratio.
  • Plume already handles the second break in the record, from November 2026, when Suomi NPP went dark.
  • The "this month" view compares a half-finished month with the same days in past years, so a month still under way doesn't look quiet.

What did we consider?

  • Plume counts satellite detections, which is different from burned area, and labels them that way.
  • Only Suomi NPP is used for the VIIRS part of the record. Each extra satellite adds more passes overhead and would raise the counts even when no more is burning.
  • Colors come from colorblind-safe palettes, and every square in the calendar works with a keyboard.
  • Two regions are loaded today, California and Argentina's Gran Chaco. Adding another takes one configuration entry and a rerun of the pipeline.

What tools did we use?

  • Python with pandas, NumPy and DuckDB for the data pipeline, with results stored as Parquet files
  • FastAPI for the server
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for the web app
  • pytest for testing
  • NASA FIRMS archives for MODIS Collection 6.1, VIIRS Suomi NPP and VIIRS NOAA-20, plus the FIRMS API for recent detections

Use of AI

We used Claude Code to help write, debug and review code. We reviewed and tested its output ourselves. The app makes no AI calls, and every number it shows comes from the satellite data. We used no AI-generated images and no NASA logos or branding.
